why: A tight single-weight hero serif over a newsroom grotesque, so the headline owns all the contrast.
A dense 900 roman over an American gothic gives the skeleton of a broadsheet without quoting one.
A compressed didone beside a normal-width grotesque lets long headlines run huge while the body stays human.
One Caslon in two widths: the squeezed cut carries long heads, the roomy cut carries the reading.
A narrow headline cut and its large-x-height text partner, built to hold many words in tight columns.
Trade-gothic poster energy over a fine screen serif; the sizes are far apart so the two never compete.
A 19th-century textbook roman beside a 20th-century trade gothic, so the page reads as an archive that has been re-edited.
Times worn down by repeated scanning, labelled by a clean mono, says document and evidence at once.
Tiny caps and tight heavy weights, sized up 1.3x, sit on a serif drawn purely for long reading.
A compressed classic gothic over a calm Charter-style roman, the old newspaper recipe and still the strongest one.
A headline gothic over a wedge-serif text face, which has more edge than the usual condensed-plus-bookish mix.
A real newspaper nameplate over a serious front-page roman; use the blackletter once, for the masthead only.
A very narrow title face lets a long line run at full bleed, and a dark, even serif anchors it.
A working condensed in mixed case above a curly Spanish roman: blunt headline, expensive paragraph.
Scotch-roman ball terminals at 800 against a clean modern grotesque keep the richness in the headline.
A didone-flavoured mono italic as a headline is rare; a warm grotesque stops it reading as code.
A tall narrow serif with one weight fits more words at display size, and an offbeat grotesque answers it.
One Bodoni, two optical sizes: opsz 96 for razor headlines, opsz 11 for a text cut sturdy enough to read.
The huge optical range is the design: hairline masthead at opsz 1200, soft text at opsz 14, narrowed at the top.
A proper poster black against a plain regular: one American gothic can run a whole newspaper.
Drawn for a news group, it holds a masthead at 900 and a product UI at 400 without a second face.
Crisp at black weight and calm at light, with the looped italic ampersand as the single flourish.
A rare heavy oldstyle: 900 headlines keep the pen rhythm of the 400 text, so hierarchy comes from weight alone.
Trade Gothic energy on a width axis: condensed 700 for heads, standard 400 for text.
A condensed sans with an opinion in every letter: narrow black headlines, roomy regular text.
Width does the hierarchy: 62.5 for tall black headlines, 100 for reading, 150 for a stretched label.
Small ink traps give the headline a hacker-newspaper feel, and a snappy neutral keeps the body out of the way.
A full-range Anton with a huge x-height over a wedge serif: loud head, literate body.
An uneven grotesque headline above a screen slab flips the usual order, with the personality left in the sans.
A wide fat face with razor hairlines reads as a masthead; the plain gothic body gives it something to push against.
A swash-Q Baskerville kept large, over a civic grotesque that makes it look deliberate and not antique.
An italic Bodoni headline over a tight Swiss-leaning sans, with all the romance held in one line.
Thick-thin calligraphy without serifs against a Futura skeleton, two ideas of elegance a generation apart.
Inscriptional capitals with open tracking over a light screen serif: quiet authority for houses and foundations.

Light Roman capitals over a roomy Caslon, tracked out, for fashion houses and galleries.
